source.title: Language Models Improve When Pretraining Data Matches Target Tasks
source.authors: David Mizrahi; Anders Boesen Lindbo Larsen; Jesse Allardice; Suzie Petryk; Yuri Gorokhov; Jeffrey Li; Alex Fang; Josh Gardner; Tom Gunter; Afshin Dehghan

record.tranche_reason: The study trains language models across model-size and token-count configurations, measures validation loss, and fits a Chinchilla-style scaling-law form to it, applying the loss-scaling measurement in new data-selection settings.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports numerous data-selection and benchmark results. Rows below retain results relevant to loss scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, downstream accuracy scaling, and related scale-dependent filtering. Values cited only from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's main aim is data selection, and it uses scaling laws mainly as a tool for compute multipliers. It still fits the Hoffmann-form loss law, L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, with Besiroglu-style Huber fitting on its own grid of 53 models per dataset. It reports its own results on fit quality (Table 12), the compute-optimal D/N ratio (App. D.1) and the predictability of loss-to-accuracy mapping (App. C.1, C.4). These bear on V1, V3, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is wrong about the paper's focus. The authors conclude that targeting pretraining data at benchmarks (BETR) gives 1.8–2.8x compute multipliers over baselines (4.7x over no filtering). They also conclude that optimising for Core narrows capabilities on held-out tasks, and that optimal filtering predictably becomes less strict with scale. Scaling laws serve as the comparison tool. The 10–12 tokens-per-parameter ratio is a side finding in the appendix.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a Chinchilla-style loss function and model-size/token sweeps, but applies them to compare data-selection settings and also predicts benchmark accuracy through a separate BPB-to-accuracy fit. It uses its own fitting procedure and tested data/model grid.
record.method_sensitivity: The compute-optimal filtering trend varies by data pool (Fopt ∝ C^0.25 for Nemotron-CC and C^0.14 for DCLM-RefinedWeb) and differs between compute-optimal training and fixed-model-size token scaling. The paper also reports irregular standard MMLU accuracy-to-BPB behavior but smoother MMLU-Direct behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute-optimal BETR filtering rate rises as a power of compute: C^0.25 on Nemotron-CC, C^0.14 on DCLM-RefinedWeb, and D^0.13 at a fixed 6.6B model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal fraction of pretraining data retained by quality filtering grows with compute, at a rate that depends on the data pool and training regime.

record.problems: The scaling evidence comes from a finite grid spanning 50M to 6.6B parameters and 1.1B to 152B training tokens; the paper does not report held-out extrapolation tests from small runs to much larger runs. Validation-loss scaling is fit separately by dataset, and the authors note that training loss is not suitable for comparing different datasets. The experiments are limited to English text, and the paper reports that standard MMLU accuracy-to-BPB patterns are irregular.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows were omitted. The paper reports more per-benchmark compute multipliers and individual-task outcomes; only explicit examples and the Core-average multiplier are retained here, because the remaining task-level results are not needed to represent the reported aggregate downstream-scaling finding.

untested.parts: There is no held-out comparison of small-run fits against much larger observed runs. Predictions up to 1e23 FLOPs (Figs 21, 10) are not checked against observed runs.
Separate fitted exponents for N_opt(C) and D_opt(C) are not reported.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Only English text pretraining is studied: no other modalities, repeated data or fine-tuning.

missing.what: Sigmoid accuracy-from-BPB fit errors per benchmark (MAE about 0.002–0.011), evidence for V6 predictability
Loss-to-accuracy relation varies significantly across data pools, selection methods and filtering rates
Validation-loss fit parameters and MAE (e.g. α≈0.30, β≈0.33, MAE≈0.022)
Each benchmark's BPB fit has slightly different compute-optimal configurations

record.verdict_notes: The study fits per-dataset laws with inverse-density reweighting and bootstrap. Its compute range is about 3 orders of magnitude. The 7B-10x runs at 6e22 FLOPs are not used to check extrapolation. r3 and r4 are method comparisons and should be unlinked from V6.

versions.untested_parts: The reported validation-loss fits cover the study's tested English-text models, data pools, and compute range; they do not establish the claim for other modalities or regimes.

The study fits curves to its model grid and uses them to predict across compute budgets, but does not report a test in which fits from small runs are evaluated against held-out runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study reports compute-optimal token-to-parameter ratios and their trend, but does not give separate fitted growth exponents for parameter count and token count.
No comparison varies architecture at a fixed parameter count to measure the effect of depth, width, or other architecture details.
The experiments use English text and do not test other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The downstream tests cover the paper's benchmark suite and its stated evaluation formats, not downstream tasks in general.

The reported compute-optimal ratio differs from the cited Hoffmann et al. ratio, but the study does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, or fitting method to establish sensitivity to those choices, nor does it test whether curves bend at extreme scales.

rows.subject: All trained language models (11 datasets)
rows.operation_detail: Trained models across model-size and token-count configurations; fitted validation loss as a function of parameters and training tokens.
rows.value: The study fits the stated power-law form to validation loss; it reports fitted curves for each dataset.
rows.uncertainty: 4000 bootstrap resamplings; 95% confidence intervals are reported for fitted parameters and curves.
rows.note: The authors state that training loss is not suitable for comparing different datasets, but fit validation-loss scaling separately for each dataset. The grid and reported compute range are finite.
rows.check: The value gives no numbers. Table 12 reports validation-loss fits, e.g. Nemotron-CC BETR Top 10%: α≈0.31, β≈0.33, MAE 0.021. Across filters MAE is about 0.021–0.022. The fit spans about 3 orders of compute (6e18–6e21 FLOPs), which should be noted.

rows.subject: Compute-optimal models across data pools and selection methods
rows.size_stated: 50M to 6.6B parameters in the scaling experiments
rows.operation_detail: Derived compute-optimal model sizes and token counts from fitted loss scaling laws, then examined the token-to-parameter ratio across compute.

conditions.value: No Filter, DCLM-Baseline, Nemotron-CC HQ, BETR Target-Noncore, BETR Target-Core, where applicable

rows.measure: Compute-optimal training tokens per parameter, D/Nopt
rows.baseline: Hoffmann et al. ratio of approximately 20 tokens per parameter, as cited by the authors
rows.value: Ratios are typically around 10–12 tokens per parameter; the authors report no significant trend with increasing compute and similar ratios across data-selection methods within uncertainty bounds.
rows.note: The stable ratio is consistent with parameter count and token count growing at similar rates in the tested range. The reported ratio is lower than the approximately 20-token ratio cited for Hoffmann et al.
rows.check: The state is right. The ~20 Chinchilla ratio is a cited value used only as a reference, not a baseline. Read for V3, the stable ratio supports equal growth of N and D (the Hoffmann form). Read for V7, the lower level of 10–12 tokens per parameter shows setup dependence.

rows.subject: BETR Target-Core models on DCLM-RefinedWeb
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal Core benchmark accuracy scaling against the unfiltered-data baseline.
rows.measure: Core average benchmark accuracy, summarized as a compute multiplier
rows.uncertainty: Bootstrap uncertainty is used for the scaling comparisons; no interval for this multiplier is stated here.
rows.note: The multiplier summarizes accuracy-versus-compute scaling, not a direct validation-loss comparison.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (BETR) against No Filter as a compute multiplier. It does not measure whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss, so it should not be linked to V6.

rows.subject: BETR Target-Core models on Nemotron-CC
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal Core benchmark accuracy scaling against the unfiltered-data baseline.
rows.measure: Core average benchmark accuracy, summarized as a compute multiplier
rows.uncertainty: Bootstrap uncertainty is used for the scaling comparisons; no interval for this multiplier is stated here.
rows.note: The paper also reports that per-benchmark compute multipliers vary substantially; its text gives 10.4x for ARC-Easy, 9.5x for PIQA, 2.8x for WebQuestions, and 1.8x for Winogrande on Nemotron-CC.
rows.check: Same issue as r3: a method comparison (4.7x in Table 5), not a test of downstream predictability.

rows.subject: Models evaluated on MMLU and MMLU-Direct
rows.size_stated: 50M to 6.6B parameters in the scaling experiments
rows.operation_detail: Compared MMLU accuracy-to-bits-per-byte patterns under the standard answer-by-reference format and the MMLU-Direct reformulation.
rows.measure: Regularity of accuracy as a function of benchmark bits-per-byte
rows.value: Standard MMLU shows irregular and unpredictable accuracy-to-BPB patterns; MMLU-Direct shows a smooth, predictable relationship. The authors report a strong monotonic correlation between the two formats.
rows.note: This finding qualifies downstream predictability by evaluation format; subsequent scaling analyses use MMLU-Direct.
rows.check: Correct as recorded. The text adds that MMLU-Direct gives lower absolute accuracy above 1e21 FLOPs.

rows.subject: BETR Target-Core models on Nemotron-CC
rows.operation_detail: Trained models at four document-token filtering rates and fitted the compute-dependent optimal retention rate.
rows.measure: Optimal percentage of tokens retained as a function of compute
rows.value: Fopt(C) = 4 × 10−5 C^0.25; the reported optimal rate shifts from 3% below 10^21 FLOPs, to 10% around 10^22 FLOPs, to 30% beyond 10^23 FLOPs.
rows.uncertainty: The probability of each rate being optimal is estimated from bootstrap distributions; no interval for the exponent is stated.
rows.note: This concerns optimal data filtering, not the parameter/token allocation named by V3.
rows.check: Concerns the filtering-rate law, not a claim version; it belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: BETR Target-Core models on DCLM-RefinedWeb
rows.operation_detail: Fitted the compute-dependent optimal retention rate for BETR-filtered data.
rows.measure: Optimal percentage of tokens retained as a function of compute
rows.value: Fopt(C) = 6 × 10−3 C^0.14; at 10^23 FLOPs the optimal rate is predicted to be Top 10%.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown for scaling curves; no interval for the exponent is stated.
rows.note: The authors report a less pronounced shift toward lighter filtering than on Nemotron-CC.
rows.check: Concerns the filtering-rate law, not a claim version.

rows.subject: 6.6B-parameter BETR Target-Core models on Nemotron-CC
rows.operation_detail: Varied training tokens at fixed model size and fitted the optimal filtering rate.
rows.measure: Optimal percentage of tokens retained as a function of training tokens
rows.value: Fopt(D) = 0.26 × D^0.13; a shift from 3% to 10% filtering occurs as training progresses, with no 10%-to-30% transition in the studied range.
rows.uncertainty: The probability of each rate being optimal is estimated from bootstrap distributions; no interval for the exponent is stated.
rows.note: This is a fixed-model-size filtering result, not the parameter/token allocation named by V3.
rows.check: Concerns the filtering-rate law, not a claim version.

tranche.reason: The study fits the Hoffmann joint parameter/token loss form to its own language-model validation losses and derives compute-optimal allocations. It reports fit quality and allocation behavior in addition to using scaling laws for data comparisons.
